implementation_notes: C++11 supplies the two primitives the pattern needs: std::mutex::try_lock() 'returns immediately' with true/false instead of blocking, and std::atomic<T>::compare_exchange_strong() performs the guarded check-and-set with no lock at all. The classic role structure is not a class in the standard library; the idiom is a guard clause over those primitives plus RAII (std::unique_lock<std::mutex> with std::try_to_lock) so every bail-out path releases correctly. Hand-rolled flag-and-lock versions are only justified on pre-C++11 toolchains or when a platform lock without try-semantics must be wrapped.
pitfalls: std::mutex::try_lock is allowed to fail spuriously even when the mutex is free - treat false as 'balk now', never as evidence about the guarded state.
Reading the guarded state outside the lock (or caching it in a non-atomic bool) recreates the check-then-act race the pattern removes.
Calling try_lock on a mutex the thread already owns is undefined behaviour: std::mutex is not recursive.
